Mark Goldblatt MD

Mark Goldblatt

mark_goldblatt@hms.harvard.edu
https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0391-8947

Mark Goldblatt   Psychiatrist and psychoanalyst in Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA. He is a Faculty Member of the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute and an Associate Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at Harvard Medical School. He teaches and supervises at McLean Hospital. He is also a Founding Member of the Boston Suicide Study Group, which focuses on the psychoanalytic understanding of self-destructive patients. His extensive writings reflect his interest in suicide and psychoanalysis.
NEGATIVE THERAPEUTIC REACTION, ADOLESCENTS, SUICIDE, SELF-HARM, ABRUPT TERMINATION

Psychotherapy with suicidal and self-harming young people is complex, as this population group is difficult to engage in treatment and their internal reactions may remain concealed, leading to impulsive suicide attempts or abandonment of treatment. The resulting countertransference reactions of confusion, guilt and shame are most distressing and often cause psychotherapists to avoid treating this population group. Safety concerns increase when self-destructive patients abandon therapy, or their condition worsens despite the therapist's best efforts. The vicissitudes of the adolescent developmental process suggest that, in some cases, withholding information, rejection of the therapist's caring interventions, and abrupt termination of treatment arise from the need for separation and independence and are ego syntonic and therefore suicide protecting. In other cases, the risk for suicide may be increased because of the transference experience of hostile abandonment. A negative therapeutic reaction (NTR) is a disturbing development in the course of psychotherapy that has not been adequately explained in the treatment of suicidal young people. This article is a consideration of whether these negative reactions associated with abrupt, unplanned terminations, in the treatment of self-destructive young people, should appropriately be thought of as an NTR or as a developmental stage in separation.

LITERATURE, FORM, FICTION, CHARACTER, TRANSFERENCE, THERAPEUTIC CHANGE, PSYCHIC REALITY, PSYCHIC TRUTH

In this paper, the author looks at some central psychoanalytic themes through the lens of literature. In literary criticism, it is clear that we construct a meaning with the help of certain formal principles. In literature, we also know that fiction differs from documentary or scientific prose. The literary critic thinks that, specifically in fiction, one may find new formal principles and, through that, new perspectives on reality. With the help of these literary constructs, the author looks at character, transference, therapeutic change and truth/reality in psychoanalysis. The argument is elaborated in relation to a clinical example.

Laurence Spurling

Laurence Spurling

lspsychotherapy1@gmail.com

Laurence Spurling   Psychoanalytic psychotherapist in private practice and SeniorMember of the British Psychotherapy Foundation. He is director of the BPF Supervision Skills course. He has written “An Introduction to Psychodynamic Counselling” (Palgrave, 2004) and “The Psychoanalytic Craft”, (Palgrave, 2015) and articles on variousaspects of clinical practice.
SUPERVISION, SELF-REFLECTION, DEVELOPMENT, TEACHING

In clinical practice, there is a well-established developmental path from beginner to post-qualification and on to some form of expertise or mastery. In this paper, I explore whether the outline of a similar pathway could be mapped out for analytic supervision. For the clinician, a key element in becoming more competent and skilled is the capacity to reflect on one's work and learn from experience. To do that the clinician learns to develop a form of internal conversation which orients them to the work. I argue that an important developmental step for the supervisor is to acquire a similar capacity, which I call the supervisor's internal monologue. In this paper, I illustrate what I mean by the supervisor's internal monologue and discuss some of its functions and characteristics.

‘Meeting the Client where they are Rather than Where I'm At’: A Qualitative Survey Exploring CBT and Psychodynamic Therapist Perceptions of Psychotherapy Integration

Greta Kaluzeviciute-Moreton and Christopher Lloyd

Christopher Lloyd

greta.kaluzeviciute@fsf.vu.lt

Christopher Lloyd   Lecturer in Psychology and BPS Chartered and HCPC registered Counselling Psychologist. He holds a DProf in Counselling Psychology. He has worked in both National Health Service (NHS) and charity services for over a decade and currently works in international private practice. He undertakes university teaching and peer reviewed research and has a particular interest in innovative and novel qualitative methods, such as qualitative surveys and story completion.
PSYCHOTHERAPY INTEGRATION, PSYCHOANALYSIS, PSYCHODYNAMIC THERAPY, COGNITIVE BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY, THERAPIST ATTITUDES

This qualitative study explored therapists' attitudes towards psychotherapy integration. Twenty-nine psychoanalytic/psychodynamic and cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) therapists completed an open-ended survey that focused on their personal understanding of psychotherapy integration, examples from their own practice and reflections on improving integrative therapy. Participants were also encouraged to share attitudes and perceptions towards the other therapeutic paradigm (CBT towards psychoanalysis, and vice versa). Thematic analysis revealed three main themes: (1) Positive perceptions and benefits of psychotherapy integration, (2) Negative perceptions and challenges of psychotherapy integration and (3) Proposals for strengthening integration in clinical practice. While most participants had a strong allegiance to their modality, they recognised the need for flexibility and additional techniques from other paradigms to address individual client needs. However, participants raised concerns about the level of knowledge required for integrative work and the epistemological compatibility between CBT and psychoanalysis. Some responses reflected the ongoing ‘turf wars’ between the two paradigms, with some referring to ‘outdated’ psychoanalytic ideas and ‘dogmatic’ evidence-based hierarchies. Suggestions were made for further development of psychotherapy integration during the training and post-qualification. The study reflects a generally positive outlook towards integration while recognising the challenges as well as the continuing resistances between CBT and psychoanalytic paradigms.

Jonathan Day

Jonathan Day

newdaypsychotherapy@outlook.com

Jonathan Day   Qualified and registered Counselling Psychologist (HCPC). He practices clinically in an NHS specialist Mentalisation-Based Therapy service. His current professional interests include health inequalities, complex trauma, critical psychopathology, contemporary relational psychoanalysis and consultation work.
PSYCHODYNAMIC CONSULTATION, HOMELESSNESS, UNHOUSED MINDS, FORENSIC, ANTI-SOCIAL

People experiencing homelessness are subject to entrenched health inequalities and obstacles to accessing care. Numerous studies have highlighted that structural and organisational obstacles result in people experiencing homelessness living with unmet healthcare needs. Over time, this is associated with a reduced life expectancy compared with the national average in the UK. Although combating health inequalities has become a mandate for many healthcare providers, attempts to improve parity and access for people experiencing homelessness has stalled. This article utilises a case study method to highlight instances of psycho-social exclusion that homeless patients can be subject to and examples where healthcare staff can collude in this exclusion. The article concludes with highlighting the benefits of psychologically informed staff consultation, which creates reflective spaces to gain a better understanding of people experiencing multiple disadvantage and exclusion. In addition, staff consultation allows space to process feelings that are stoked in professionals who struggle to comprehend why it is difficult for some people to accept offers of care.

Experiences of Working-Age Adults with Depression of Psychodynamic Couple Therapy: A Thematic Analysis Using a Phenomenological Approach

Ilaria Tercelli MSc PG(Diploma) DClinPsy , Susan Mcpherson PHD and Hugo Senra PHD

Hugo Senra

itercelli@tavi-port.nhs.uk

Hugo Senra   Researcher at the Institute of Electronics and Informatics Engineering of Aveiro (IEETA), University of Aveiro (Portugal) and Honorary Lecturer in Clinical Psychology at the School of Health and Social Care, University of Essex (UK). His main research interests are adult mental health; depression; eating disorders; statistics.
COUPLE THERAPY, COUPLE, DEPRESSION, PSYCHODYNAMIC, PSYCHOTHERAPY

The current study draws on interviews with service users about their experiences to inform the practice of psychodynamic couple therapy for depression. Five participants, who had received at least six months of psychodynamic couple therapy in London (UK) for the treatment of severe distress and depression, completed a semi-structured interview. They were recruited using a purposive sampling technique. Data was analysed using a phenomenological approach to thematic analysis. Six themes were identified in relation to participants' experiences of couple therapy. Key aspects highlighted by participants include: the therapist, described as a ‘third person’, became a referee and mediated the communication within the couple, providing a different perspective, enabling a safe environment for reciprocal listening; the process of making links with the past enabled participants to understand their current behaviour as individual and dysfunctional areas as a couple; the therapist's ability to understand the couple as individuals rather than as a unified entity was key; therapist neutrality and capacity to empathise with the couple was valued by participants. The study highlighted the intertwined dynamic between relationship difficulties and depression. Participants were not able to make a clear distinction between these two experiences, and this microcosm may reflect the difficulties that clients face in accessing public services, which have historically held a more individualistic perspective of distress.

CREATIVITY, EPISTEMOPHYLIC INSTINCT, BASIC ANXIETY, SUBLIMATION, REPRESSED AGGRESSION, ENDORPHINS

This paper addresses the conditions for the development of creativity and the possible obstacles along the way. It explores conscious and unconscious mechanisms which either impede or support this process. Creativity is seen as a special case of relationships between internal and external objects, with some aspects being more consistent and others being more fluid throughout an individual's life. This paper is based on the clinical experience of psychodynamic work with clients whose psychological predicaments related to creativity impoverished different areas of their lives. The non-exhaustive list of factors to be considered when working with those clients includes a blocked epistemophilic instinct, excessively repressed aggression, and strong negative projections. A harsh superego opposing a weak ‘internal supporter’ combined with an internalised negative parental attitude to their own creativity constitutes a powerful unconscious force which prevents it from blossoming. A high level of basic anxiety, a low degree of omnipotence, and the release of endorphins in response to suffering contribute to these difficulties. Insufficient capacity to sublimate emotions and an inability to free associate prevent clients from finding the links between ideas born in the mind and their expression that could be accessed by others.

SUPERVISION, DISTURBING THERAPEUTIC EXPERIENCES, PROFESSIONAL SELF-EXPERIENCE, ENVIRONMENT OF SOLIDARITY, FINITUDE OF LIFE

Supervisees who have experienced disturbing therapeutic incidents that undermined their professional self-experiences need a supervisory environment of sameness and solidarity to process and learn from these lived experiences. To create such an environment, supervisors need to minimize the sense of safety asymmetry between themselves and their supervisees by awakening to the ‘dark,’ ominous truths of professional life. This process is facilitated by summoning memories of therapeutic experiences of failure, vulnerability and frustration at having insufficient time to achieve wished-for therapeutic goals. Awakening to these truths inspires a dark experiential mode that helps the supervisor share the supervisee's destiny and existential anxiety. Despite the contradiction between the dark and the playful, experiential modes, both are essential for creatively understanding the supervisee's disturbing therapeutic experiences and learning from them. Moreover, when these modes are interwoven, they enrich and strengthen the supervisory process by diversifying the supervisory dyad's ways of perceiving the unfolding therapeutic interaction and of coping with supervisory challenges.

Jo Hopkins   Psychodynamic counsellor. She qualified with the Postgraduate Diploma in Counselling at the University of Reading in 2012 and is an accredited member of the BACP. She completed an infant observation at the British Psychotherapy Foundation in 2020. She works in private practice in Reading and is a seminar leader and supervisor on the Diploma in Psychodynamic Counselling at Basingstoke Counselling Service.
SIGHT-IMPAIRMENT, DISAVOWAL, MULTI-SENSORY, SOMATIC, PRIMITIVE DEFENCES, OBSERVATION

The author reflects on the experience of conducting an infant observation from their perspective of having a sight impairment encapsulated in the phrase ‘seeing feelingly’ taken from Shakespeare's play King Lear. The multi-sensory and somatic world of the infant is explored where sight is secondary to touch in early infancy and how this reflects something of the observer's way of experiencing the world. The impact of disability on how the author sees themselves and is seen by others is discussed in terms of the defences of projection, projective identification and disavowal. The COVID-19 pandemic and the necessity of remote observations via video link add another angle from which emotional connection is explored, leading the author to conclude that, although greater visual clarity was gained, emotional contact was diminished. The paradox of a sight-impaired person ‘observing’ challenges the privileging of the sense of sight, suggesting that a more multi-sensory approach could be of benefit to the conduct of infant observations. In addition, the very title ‘infant observation’ might deter others with sight impairment from participation.

Harriet Mossop

Harriet Mossop

Colchester, UK
hm21886@essex.ac.uk

Harriet Mossop  

The deep unconscious contact of the psychotherapy consulting room can be risky for both patient and therapist; patients of registered psychotherapists in the UK are protected by codes of ethics and complaints processes developed and enforced by the psychotherapy and counselling professional bodies (or the National Health Service (NHS), for patients in the public system). This edited collection of essays provides critical perspectives on professional complaint processes, starting from the personal experiences of patient complaints received by its editors, experienced clinicians Adah Sachs and Valerie Sinason.

There is currently little literature on professional complaints in psychotherapy; this collection is especially unusual because it foregrounds the risk that a patient's unconscious aggression poses to therapists when magnified through the lens of a professional complaint and subsequent misconduct process and asks what further protection therapists need. It is divided into three parts: clinicians' personal accounts of complaints, historical perspectives and proposals for future reform.

In Part I, the contributors vividly set out several examples of patient complaints about their therapists from the perspective of the therapist. We hear from therapists who have been accused by their patients of lacking professional care, of being unqualified to practice and even of physical and sexual abuse. The clinicians describe their shock and hurt at being accused: Sachs ‘couldn't think at all’ (p. 4); another therapist ‘was….bombarded by un-wanted communications from [the patient] and … it was beginning to make [her] ill.’ (p. 30); a third felt ‘split into fragments’ (p. 49). The reader is left with a vivid impression of how shaming it can be for a therapist to receive a complaint from a patient, and how deeply the risk to their professional reputations and livelihoods can be felt, even when the allegations are obviously false. The contributors acknowledge that complaints are often made by vulnerable patients and can be a useful source of information about the patients' unconscious processes. However, they are concerned that the current legalistic and adversarial processes for handling complaints may cause clients to lose the therapeutic relationship unnecessarily and may not protect the patients' interests in some cases, for example, when a third party makes a complaint. They also collectively put forward the key arguments of the book: that the current professional misconduct processes unnecessarily expose therapists to false complaints and that professional bodies should protect their therapists more.

SHAME, GAZE, OBJECT A, LACAN, SUBJECT, LACK, AFFECT

This paper proposes a Lacanian theory of shame linked to the era of Lacan's work starting with Seminar X and the invention of the object a. From a Lacanian perspective, shame is not evoked by the exposure of a deficit, but rather by the exposure and witnessing of the divided subject's constitutive lack. This paper proposes that the affect of shame is an index pointing to the divided subject's structural lack when it is exposed and witnessed by object a instantiated as the gaze of the scopic drive and the voice of the invocatory drive. Since shame can freeze speech as well as provoke flight from the analytic work, we suggest that it is helpful for the clinician to understand how the structure of shame manifests in the patient's speech and in the transference. Clinical examples are given throughout. The paper concludes with a case discussion of Lacanian analytic work with a female patient confronted with multiple existential dilemmas that evoked shame in relationship to her body, sexuality and death.

SUPERVISION, DIALECTIC, DIALOGUE, MUTUAL RECOGNITION, ACKNOWLEDGING VULNERABILITY

Whereas the therapeutic action centres on emotional participation and containment of the patient's intolerable experiences, the supervisory action centres on interpreting the reconstructed therapeutic reality. Since the emergent interpretation is subjective and contextual, it requires processing in a dialogue between the supervisor and the supervisee. However, their existential need to define and assert themselves as professionals often urges them to highlight the differences between their perceptions and beliefs and keenly convince each other. Uncontained, this dialectical tension might disrupt the supervisory process and the participants’ well-being. Despite the existential urges, when the supervisor and the supervisee recognize and validate each other as independent and autonomous professionals, they can restrain their competitiveness, maintain a productive dialectical dialogue, achieve creative and integrated understandings of the therapeutic process and consolidate their professional identities. Moreover, despite the hierarchical supervisory relationship, acknowledging their vulnerability helps supervisors recognize and validate their supervisees and facilitate the dialectical supervisory dialogue.

The purpose of this article is to recount the early history of the Rorschach’s inkblots test in Europe and the USA; its subsequent application in highlighting the ill effects on children of bombing during the Second World War; its wartime use in selecting military personnel; its post-war use in selecting patients for psychotherapy at the Tavistock Clinic in London and subsequent decline in this use of Rorschach’s inkblots in favour of focus on the psychotherapy patient’s transference experience of the psychotherapist treating them. The article ends with evidence of interest, beyond psychotherapy, in Rorschach’s inkblots and with the implications of this for the author’s principal conclusion regarding the value of these inkblots in evoking the free association and conversation crucial to psychotherapy.

Many individuals who have been through transition struggle to obtain the necessary medical and psychological support. This paper explores the importance of psychological support for post-transition individuals. In my experience, there is a subgroup of patients who struggle to come to terms with life post-transition, particularly the losses involved. They remain stuck in the mourning process. There is a loss of fantasies regarding an ideal transition, and the gap between the hoped-for transition outcomes and the post-transition reality can be painfully large. In addition, issues that the transition was meant to address remain in some form for some people, and they may also be haunted by misgivings about how the transition occurred. This paper employs a heavily anonymised composite case to illustrate and elaborate on how these issues emerged and were dealt with in the context of a psychotherapeutic process. Working through issues that led to transition and grievances about perceived and actual failures in care from the past allowed the patient to mourn the loss of her pre-transition image. The patient was able to come to terms with the reality of her transfer from male to trans-female and her body and life post-transition and to shift from a preoccupation with the past to move on with her life.

Psychotherapy is broadly concerned with secrets. Often our clients bring us things which they have never told anyone, subjects they have felt unable to broach. What happens in the relationship when a secret is uncovered? In this article, I discuss how one’s secrets finally being uncovered can invoke shame. However, the shame of being seen in a new way can also create an opening that allows for a deeper intersubjective experience to unfold. Using Sartre’s concept of the gaze of the other alongside Merleau-Ponty’s ideas of dehiscence, visibility/invisibility and intertwining, I explore the meaning of secrecy, guilt and shame for both therapist and client within the therapeutic relationship.

General Comments

Referral and presenting problem: R sought help himself. The ending of a relationship with a young ‘ideal’ woman seems to have been traumatic for him—he then left his job, ‘literally slamming the door behind him’ and lacked a steady income. Representing himself as a ‘two-time loser’, he began psychotherapy with a concrete, rather magical, wish to have these losses restored to him. R does not seem to have much insight into his contribution to the breakup. What is conveyed is a sense of grievance, anger and a passive position of things happening to him, a loser, perhaps the adoption of a victim stance.

History: R has been troubled for some years—there is some evidence of him as a troubled child. R is the first and eldest son with a considerably younger brother. I wonder whether there were other pregnancies or miscarriages in this significant gap between the children's births. R's father died when he was a teenager. His representation of his father is of ‘a loser’ and ‘alcoholic’. We do not know the exact nature of the child rearing practices. Was there physical or verbal beating by the father? Was R isolated as punishment, for example, sent to his room? Was he deprived of privileges as punishment? The representation of mother is one of indifference to her son's suffering; we also hear how she considered his punishment ‘natural and necessary’ and did not intervene to protect him. So, both parents, it seemed, contributed to R's sense of himself as a ‘two-time loser.’

Then we hear that R is sent to weekly boarding school at a very young age, preschool age—what age? As a child analyst, for that matter any analyst, this seems particularly important to know. At school, R displaces, re-enacts and repeats his conflicts with his father and mother, provoking older children. It is unknown whether he remains at boarding school during his adolescence when his father dies.

R's sense of self is fragile—he follows others’ desire and seems to resort to how others see him, defining himself from the outside in, manifesting some aspects of a false self. R has aspirations, yet is plagued by his repeated difficulties at work and in his intimate relationships. He falls in love, then becomes disappointed, ending the relationship, thus indicating a difficulty in moving beyond idealisation.

Psychodynamic psychotherapy does not feature in current treatment guidelines for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in the United Kingdom. However, there is some psychoanalytic understanding of the disorder, which is corroborated in current neuroscientific theory, and supports clinicians in thinking beyond the behaviourally biased diagnosis and treatment models. One of the core features of ADHD is distortions in chronoception. This clinical paper therefore explores the psychoanalytic and neuroscientific theories of time perception as a way of exploring a discrete element of the complex idea of executive functioning more generally. It supports therapists approaching such executive dysfunction and to reconsider the treatment guidelines. A case example is used to explore how a transference-, affect- and relationally-focussed therapy can effect lasting change for people with ADHD in a way that behavioural and medication approaches do not. It is argued that such an intervention can improve oscillatory attention between subjective- and objective-time and increase the capacity to self-contain emotions. This brings patients into alignment with reality and restarts their psychic development towards themselves, others, the parental couple and grieving, which stalled in infancy. The internalised schema of the 50-minute therapy session also provides a frame of reference for future tasks.

Carol Leader  

In an author's note to Blake’s Job: Adventures in Becoming, Jason Wright tells us the story of how he came to leave a theatre career after suffering a spinal injury in a car accident at the age of 28. Not long afterwards, he began to train as a psychotherapist, having discovered an interest in the works of C. G. Jung and William Blake. Then, in the 1990s, as a result of a strange encounter in Bloomsbury, he was able to make a complete series of picture slides from a copy of Blake's Illustrations of the Book of Job, taken from the original 19th C etched plates. These images have informed much of Wright's therapeutic work and thinking since then. They are the core of this marvellous and complex book that will be a resource to psychotherapy and psychoanalytic practitioners alike, as well as all those interested in William Blake's contribution regarding addictive and repetitive states of mind and body.

Illustrations of the Book of Job was Blake's final completed work before he died in 1827. It offers the clearest rendition of his mythological system leading to expanded spiritual perception. At the core of this system is the human struggle between Human Imagination and an inner accusatory voice that Blake had a number of names for: ‘Satan’, ‘Error’, ‘Eternal Death’, ‘one-fold vision’. This is a mental state of great omnipotence that is relationally and spiritually blind. Blake was plagued by this inner state for a great deal of his life. He knew that it daily crucified imaginative life. He used the archetypal story of Job to demonstrate the transformative journey that can lead us out of ‘Error’ and ‘Eternal Death’ into the expanded perceptual experience of ‘Eternal Life’ or ‘four-fold vision’.

Wright brings Blake's visionary insights into the 21st century, demonstrating their continual relevance in dealing with the traumas of human experience, the conflictual nature of our inner worlds and humanity's increasingly mindless treatment of planetary resources. At the beginning of an excellent introduction, Wright lays out the book's central purpose:

(to) use Blake's Illustrations of the Book of Job (1825) to describe what I see as a move from a consciousness of exploitation to a consciousness of resonance. I would like to encourage a movement from the assumption that as individuals and as a species we can exploit the context in which we live, to the understanding that we are a participatory component in a wider process of becoming.

Initially, like the author of this clinical material, I was ‘baffled and lost,’ as to how to think about this material, but starting with the opening statement that the patient was shocked, by his experience of a breakup in his relationship, presumably he had not expected it, as it had seemed an ideal match. I thought I would quote a passage from one of John Steiner's (2023) paper about mourning, with a quote by the singer Bruce Springsteen:

The trick is you have to turn your ghosts into ancestors. Ghosts haunt you. Ancestors walk alongside you and provide you with comfort and a vision of life that’s going to be your own. My father walks alongside me as my ancestor now. It took a long time for that to happen.

The background, early history, presentation, current life circumstances and the analytic session presented to us in this vignette, all in their entirety, seem very much to resonate with the themes of the conference today, ‘Continuity and Disruption.’

Mr R was shocked and traumatised by the experience of breakdown and loss in his relationships, both personal and professional. That was a significant and decisive moment in his life that motivated him to seek psychotherapeutic help. Usefully, he brought with him some rudimentary but an important awareness and understanding of his difficulties: A ‘deficit’ in his ability to maintain relationships; a combination of ‘vexation and conviction’ about his failures; an inner awareness of his ‘insufficient development’; a ‘compulsive search’ in various object-related experiences for answers to the questions about the painful difficulties in his emotional life which plagued him. However, the implicit and disguised demand for losses to be recovered and restored also suggested a severe lack of psychic resources to repair his damaged internal objects and his relationships with him. From his perspective, closeness and intimacy evaded him. Dependency posed danger and disappointment for him. Others exuded the kind of success he could only imitate. Freedom and spontaneity were qualities he could not own.

I think the summary of Mr R's experiences and events in his childhood and later development helps the therapist and us to contextualise and map out his inner world. It is clear that he found his objects were callous and cold towards him. An alcoholic father who punished him for disobedience, and a mother who was indifferent to suffering left him with bitterness, rage and helplessness. To overcome this inner plight and turmoil, he devised a life plan: Idealised objects in the form of a house, an expensive car and a beautiful wife. Yet, in life and in therapy, despite a façade of competence and an apparent capacity to cope with his difficulties, he was stuck in circular thoughts and repetitive behaviour. He was inhibited and fearful of the prospect of change and considered himself an imposter who struggled to engage and make any meaningful contact with his objects.

Paddy Farr  

Lara Sheehi and Stephen Sheehi's (2022) book, Psychoanalysis Under Occupation, is a timely and critically important work on the struggles faced by Palestinian clinicians. The book highlights multiple difficulties associated with both psychotherapy practice and social struggle through a nuanced and powerful exposition of psychoanalytic theory as it applies to Palestine. Through interviews with Palestinian clinicians on their clinical cases, Sheehi and Sheehi interrogate psychoanalytic process under the gaze of Israeli clinical supervisors. They find that within Israeli society, there are no bounds of the apartheid state as it exercises racialized power dynamics equally over both Palestinian clinician and patient alike. On the one hand, violent conditions faced by Palestinians through apartheid, occupation and settler colonialism is a material violence against their bodies. However, Israeli violence against Palestinians is not isolated to the world outside but likewise affects psychic structure. Thus, they argue, the only true means to a psychoanalytic treatment for Palestinians is through a material resistance to occupation, apartheid and settler colonialism for the liberation of Palestine.

Drawing strong influence from psychoanalyst Franz Fanon, Sheehi and Sheehi argue that under the violence of settler colonialism, psychological difficulties are shaped by colonial power structures over patients. Fanon points to how this establishes an alienation within the psyche of the colonized subject where the material conditions of settler colonialism are dissociated from. Accordingly, a central goal of Fanonian psychoanalytic practice is to bring into consciousness the sociogenic origin of psychological suffering thus laying bare the material reality of the colonial rule. Fanon names this process disalienation. Describing Fanon's disalienation, Sheehi and Sheehi explicate how the process intends to produce ‘a consciousness in the colonial patient, an awareness that they are sociogenic subjects forged by the violence pressed upon them and the material of their individual and collective subjectivity that resides in their body and psyche’ (Sheehi & Sheehi, 2022, 67). And yet, merely bringing consciousness of the sociogenic roots of alienation in not enough. The ultimate goal of the Fanonian psychoanalytic project is to engage the patient in decolonial struggle for both the psyche and the land, for without material liberation from the conditions of settler colonialism, the psyche is bounded by material violence. Through their interviews, they find that Fanonian psychoanalysis is thriving among Palestinian clinicians, with all of the clinicians interviewed identifying themselves as Fanonians.

Applying Psychoanalysis in Medical Care, edited by Harvey Schwartz, offers an exploration of the intersection between psychoanalytic principles and medical practice. This diverse collection of chapters, authored by professionals from various fields and countries, provides both theoretical insights and practical applications, making it a valuable resource for psychotherapists, psychoanalysts and frontline medical practitioners interested in psychoanalytic thinking.

The book begins with a chapter on psychosomatics by Joachim Kuchenhoff, setting a strong foundation by emphasising the profound link between the mind and body. This chapter, rich in complex language and detailed case studies, effectively argues for the integration of psychoanalytic thinking in medical care to address the holistic needs of patients. It highlights the significance of understanding how psychological factors can manifest physically, underscoring the need for a more comprehensive approach to patient care.

While the second chapter by Karen Proner and Valentino Ammannati, which examines the relationship between the psychoanalytic and medical models, offers valuable insights, it is somewhat less cohesive compared with other parts of the book. The chapter focuses on two case studies and the history of a training centre in Italy, providing interesting content but it could benefit from a more streamlined approach. Despite these challenges, the chapter contributes to the book's overall theme by highlighting the complexities of integrating psychoanalytic principles into diverse medical settings.

In this article, I describe my work with a patient who presented as a creative individual, yet felt like a fictional character. He was driven by a compulsion to maintain and repair broken connections at any cost, utilising his creativity for this purpose. My work with this patient, among others, allowed me to identify a group of patients who feel forced to constantly integrate and transform their external environment. I call them bricoleurs and explain the difference between bricolage and Donald Winnicott’s play and Hanna Segal’s reparation. I propose that the emergence of this psychological structure is caused by the child’s early experiences with significant objects—the childhood necessity to constantly repair and enliven the disturbed mind of the caregiver. One of the metaphors of the article is that of the machine, through which I aim to illustrate the automated internal world of the bricoleur, generated not only by the compulsion to destroy but also by the compulsion to repair and create. In the article, I highlight that working with such patients requires the analyst to carefully examine countertransference and to fully mourn the illusion created in the analytic process. I also reflect on the categories of true and false self, pondering the possibility of moving beyond the binary nature of this division.

The paradoxical title of Samuel Beckett's strange and despairing monologue, from 1965, is given in the first sentence: ‘imagination dead imagine’. By contrast, Lisa Dart's Fathom (2019), which she describes as a creative memoir about trauma, begins with a seemingly more straightforward, single-word paragraph that, in a benign circle, is repeated at the beginning of the fourth and final part of the memoir: ‘Imagine’. The contrast is telling. Meaninglessness provoked Beckett at the most profound level: For his narrator, there is ‘no trace anywhere of life’, all is lost finally either in the dark or in the unchanging whiteness. On the other hand, Dart's female narrator is a writer and a published poet who, even as she spirals into psychosis, moves ever closer to the ‘subjective certainties’ of an imagination the death of which she does not entertain. In the aftermath of her breakdown, she dreams, reminisces and tells stories. Above all, she creates from a series of evocative objects a vivid pallet of madness at the interface of colour and meaning: White snow, a royal blue duffel coat and a red scarf.

The groundwork of Fathom is chromatic, and the centrality of pictorial imagery links it to Dart's other work. Following the publication of her first poetry pamphlet, The Self in a Photograph (2005), Dart, for whom ‘colours yawn the movement of things’, brings her longing for light more clearly into view in The Linguistics of Light (2009), which includes a sequence on the paintings of Edward Hopper. In this paper, I present the idea that the documentary film My Octopus Teacher (Ehrlich & Reed) is an evocative allegory for some key threads in the ongoing learning at the heart of psychotherapy. On the one hand, the film is a narrative about a relationship formed between the narrator and documentary-maker Craig and an octopus that he encounters in daily dives in an underwater kelp forest. On the other hand, it is a story—dream of a man and an octopus who swim together in the protomental seas of the unconscious, a space where fluidity and symmetry rule, and where the boundaries between I and thou dissolve. Alongside the theme of mutual dream work, the documentary presents an evocative allegory of what it takes to practice as a therapist: the maps of our own disintegration that inform our work, and the key dispositions of learning to watch and observe and to fine tune our faith.

DREAM WORK, ULLMAN'S EXPERIENTIAL DREAMWORK GROUP APPROACH (UEDGA), LANGUAGE, CLINICAL PSYCHOLOGY, QUALITATIVE STUDY

This study explores the impact of utilizing the mother tongue on psychologists’ acquisition of proficiency in the Ullman's experiential dreamwork group approach. Employing a qualitative ethnographic methodology, the research documents the immersive training experiences within the Ullman approach, subject to subsequent analysis, by a Muslim clinical psychologist in training, whose native language is Arabic, engaging in the experiential dreamwork conducted in English. The findings confirms the pivotal role of the mother tongue in fostering group cohesion and facilitating emotional processing within the Ullman framework. Furthermore, the research underscores the significance of language in shaping the holistic learning experience, emphasizing the imperative consideration of linguistic and cultural implications inherent in this distinctive training process for clinical psychologists. A nuanced understanding of the impact of language on experiential learning enhances our comprehension of the intricate interplay between language, emotions and personal development among trainees in clinical psychology. Beyond individual learning encounters, the research prompts a broader contemplation on the incorporation of linguistic and cultural factors in the training of clinical psychologists.

Introduction

I am grateful to the British Journal of Psychotherapy for asking me to discuss this fascinating case. I write as a psychodynamically trained individual and group therapist with a longstanding interest in attachment theory applied to psychopathology and clinical practice.

I want to begin with an impossibly brief discussion of how attachment theory is a helpful paradigm for psychodynamic psychotherapists and why it represents a 21st 273 century update on classical psychoanalysis. Research based on attachment theory has provided evidence that supports Freudian claims (both Sigmund and Anna) that early parent-child attachments have a long-term influence on adult attachments, and provides an understanding of how those attachments may be repeated in adulthood, including with therapists. I think many early 20th century analysts would have been excited by the evidence from linguistic studies of attachment focused interviews that find that how people speak of themselves and others (not just the content of what they say), unconsciously reveals their state of mind with respect to relationships and vulnerability.

History

Applying attachment theory psychodynamically to S.'s history, we note an immediate sense of detachment and isolation from others, which must raise questions about who and how S. related to his parents. S. describes being a little boy whose father was away a great deal; and whose relationship with his mother is ‘normal but lacks intimacy’, as if that makes sense. S. describes feeling frightened of his father, (also described as aggressive and hostile to S.'s mother), which reminded me that chronic fear is a disorganiser of the developing mind leading to the use of dissociation and numbness as defences, which, in turn, make disorganised attachment and the use of psychotic thinking likely in adulthood. I also note the note of idealisation and minimisation of fear when S. reassures his therapist that his father was ‘not violent’.

So far, from an attachment perspective, this self-reported history conveys a strong sense of disorganised attachment insecurity. S.'s account also includes a traumatic bereavement (the strange death of his father); and there are linguistic indicators of unresolved traumatic stress, including some elements of unmentalised or psychotic thinking. We note that S. ‘knows’ that his father mistook a window for a door, implying that he knows that this death is an accident and not suicide; whereas the reality is that he cannot know this. We also note S.'s magical thought that he killed his father with his hatred; the kind of primary process thought that is characteristic of psychotic states and also of unresolved traumatic stress. Finally, we note that S. identifies with his father in that S. is a man who has violent feelings which might bring about a death.

Joanna Ryan  

This book is intended as an introduction, but not just for beginners. The brief from the publisher is to be accessible without compromising complexity and to 291 express the authors' personal views and their own contributions to the field. Hertzmann and Newbigin achieve all this and much more, showing how a psychoanalysis that moves beyond the heteronormativity and homophobia of many of its traditional theories and practices is both needed and possible. They do this by a review of past and contemporary psychoanalytic approaches, and through further chapters on internalised homophobia and present-day clinical challenges. Given the wide compass of the topic, it is necessarily compressed, but nevertheless extremely informative, with plentiful references for further reading.

The first chapter traces the social origins of concepts of homosexuality from the nineteenth century onwards and their influence on the emerging psychoanalytic concepts. This historical framing is important in underlining how extensively moral and social attitudes came to pervade supposedly ‘scientific’ psychological and psychoanalytic notions of sexuality and gender. For example, Hertzmann and Newbigin show how ‘The resulting posture of scientific certainty traditionally adopted by psychoanalysts has tended towards a view of unquestioned heteronormativity as a form of “bedrock”’ (p.113). This, they consider, led to a reluctance to critically question the basis of these theories, and to their implicit and explicit homophobia and heteronormativity. The consequent damage of this has yet to be adequately acknowledged within the profession but includes damage to patients wrongly considered perverse or otherwise pathologized; to those who were deterred from seeking help; and to those who were rendered celibate or seriously depressed, faced with the impossibility of a change in their sexuality, where this was seen (by the analyst) as a goal of treatment.

In 2019, the American Psychoanalytic Association issued an apology, printed in an appendix to this book, for the ‘discrimination and trauma caused’. The UK British Psychoanalytic Council (BPC) statement of 2021 is a much more cautious and qualified statement expressing ‘profound regret’—an instance of what the authors, quoting Jack Drescher, call psychoanalytic coyness. I would suggest there was also damage to the reputation of psychoanalysis.

OMNIPOTENCE, NEGATIVE OMNIPOTENCE, PSYCHOTIC PART OF THE PERSONALITY, OMNIPOTENT PRESERVATION OF OBJECT, SUBJECTIVE TRIANGULATION OF EGO

This paper aims to advance a theoretical and clinical perspective on the developmental origin and role of omnipotence in early object relations, and a differentiation of the adult sequelae of these maturational dynamics. The focus is on negative omnipotence as inherent in the constitution and impact of the psychotic part of the personality. The case history of the psychoanalytic psychotherapy of a man with a psychiatric diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive disorder illustrates the self and treatment defeating impact of negative omnipotence. Diplomatic therapeutic engagement, based on the understanding that these negative therapeutic dynamics represent unfinished maturational processes, is presented as enabling treatment to progress and facilitate gradual beneficial modification in the use of omnipotence intrapsychically and inter-personally.

Konstantin Nemirovskiy  

Introduction

In early 2023, the Doomsday Clock, symbolising the threat of nuclear apocalypse, showed the closest time to catastrophe in its more than 70-year history. Although its authors assess only one side of this danger, we have all felt a shift in recent years. Wars and numerous terrorist attacks around the world, pandemics and Brexit, the rise of the right-wing and populism, global warming and various environmental disasters are just a small list of ‘earth shocks’ that have already led to global change. And even if external life appears unchanged, no one can isolate themselves from these tectonic shifts inside—for example, the number of prescriptions for antidepressants in England has risen by 30% in the last 6 years (Burns, 2022).

The frangible inner world of our patients is a barometer, sometimes accurately reflecting changes in external ‘pressure’ and the clinical material presented in this issue is no exception. The patient described here has recently undergone many serious changes in his life, the psychic burden of which is weighed down by his difficult history. All three commentators accurately capture these, thoughtfully describing the various causes of the patient who is ‘hard to reach’—his ‘addiction to near death’, disorganised attachment, psychotic functioning and lack of containment. In one way or another, however, all agree that bereaved loss has a profound impact, proving Shakespeare right once again: ‘Give sorrow words: the grief that does not speak whispers the o'er-fraught heart, and bids it break’ (Shakespeare, 2004). They also agree that despite the great changes in the therapist's own life, he manages to maintain contact with the libidinal part of the patient. Whether we can save the world from catastrophe is an unanswerable question, but it is in our power to strive for peace within ourselves and our patients, neutralising external and internal destructiveness wherever possible.

I am grateful to the psychotherapist who has offered clinical material and to the three international commentators. I would also like to thank the British Journal of Psychotherapy's Editorial Board for giving me the opportunity to edit this long existing section of the Journal. Embarking on this role when ‘the times are gloomy’ again is challenging and I am greatly indebted to my predecessor, Katya Orrell for her caring guidance and powerful inspiration.

Clinical Material

(The clinical material has been carefully disguised to preserve the patient's anonymity)

S., a middle-aged man, contacted me following a professional recommendation several years ago. He did not understand his feelings towards people and saw only an attitude to events. The feeling of isolation and lack of contact to others had always been with him.

He was the only child in the family. His father served in the army and was involved in war conflicts. S. claims that his father never loved him. When he was 11, the father died after drunkenly falling from a balcony. S. was not at home at the time, but he is certain that the father ‘mistook the door for a window’ and hung for some time clinging to the edge of the balcony, but no one came to help. S. also believed that his father died because of his hatred that caused the death. He remembers his father as an intimidating and aggressive man who drank and scandalised at home but did not resort to violence.

S. described his mother to be extremely poorly but said they had a ‘normal’ relationship in which there was no intimacy of any kind. She seemed aloof, inaccessible, and always preoccupied with herself. When she was diagnosed with cancer a year ago, S. took part in her treatment with great difficulty. He would forget and try to avoid going to the doctors, or he would think that he himself had a terrible disease or that a catastrophe could happen to him. Thinking about her death, he felt galled that it would leave him indifferent.

Recalling the atmosphere of the house, he described it as follows: the father was in the living room, often drunk and discontented, the mother was in the kitchen, and S. was in his room. If they gathered at one place, there was a scandal, so he was afraid to leave his bedroom.

At the beginning of therapy, S. participated in role-playing games set in a post-apocalyptic world where he was assigned the role of a detective or a therapist. These games brought him pleasure and excitement because they were ‘easy to fall in love, get drunk and fight’.

Sophia Tickell   Masters in Psychodynamic Practice from the University of Oxford. She holds a Diploma in Psychodynamic Practice from the same institution. She works both in private practice and as a Counselling Practitioner at Cherwell Counselling. Her special interests are siblings in psychotherapy, early emotional neglect and the interface between attachment theory and psychoanalysis. SIBLINGS, PSYCHODYNAMIC THEORY, TRANSFERENCE, COUNTERTRANSFERENCE, TRAINING, PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT

This article presents the results of a Master's research study into the impact of sibling experiences on psychodynamic practitioners. Interpretative phenomenological analysis offered participating therapists an opportunity to make sense of how their own sibling experiences may have shaped their lives and work and sought to generate wider insights about sibling influence should they emerge. Data was obtained from semi-structured interviews with six psychodynamic practitioners. The research produced three major findings: that siblings do have a significant and enduring impact on the development of the self; that sibling theory and training could do more to explain this; and that the sibling legacy of both therapist and client is present in the consulting room. The article identifies important theoretical insights on how siblings shape our internal worlds and contribute to development. It argues that without understanding their own sibling material, therapists risk missing the importance of siblings in clinical work. To avoid this, training and continuing professional development bodies could give higher priority to sibling theory and clinical understanding, and supervisors and therapists could undertake to increase their own awareness of their own sibling impacts as well as those of their clients.

Emma Letley  

It is gratifying to see how, since the publication of a biography of Milner and the re-issue of editions of her main works (2010-2013), a new generation of scholars has come to the fore with work building and elaborating on these publications: one such is Emilia Halton-Hernandez. Her book considers Milner's autobiographical books and contends that her opus can be explored as positing a cure or cures, as an alternative to psychoanalytic treatment.

283

Halton-Hernandez is a meticulous and knowledgeable scholar as she charts the presence of ‘autobiographical cure’, a ‘distinctive version of object relations theory’ (p.3) in Milner's main texts. Thus, A Life of One's Own puts forward a method ‘to rival psychoanalysis’ (p.37); An Experiment in Leisure shows how the ‘answering activity’ is a ‘function found in one's own creative acts’ (p.47); Eternity's Sunrise focuses on Milner's ‘bead memories’, ‘the term bead memory embodying this notion of diary keeping as an objectification of the self that leads to a kind of transformation’ (p.51). Then, with On Not Being Able to Paint, the author structures her discussion around a series of images as she considers Milner's use of free drawing, her experiments with colour and line, the concepts of the pliable medium and, very importantly, that of the frame. In the case of The Hands of the Living God, the author demonstrates that it is ‘visual art […] that forms the heart of the account of the analysis’ (p.78) in a treatment that is ‘as much Milnerian as it is Freudian’, with analytic work proceeding ‘through relations that revolve around the patients’ autobiographical acts of drawing' (p.81).

Given these sensitively presented insights and highlights, I would also comment that, to some extent, the ‘cure’ motif is stretched and there is some repetition. (This and an incomplete index prompt me to wonder if the text could have benefitted from some more rigorous copyediting.) It is arguably worth thinking about whether ‘cure’, a term frequently used by Halton-Hernandez, is the most apposite. Modern psychoanalysis does not privilege the word, avoiding its medical, and indeed, long-term associations. Adam Phillips engages with this in his essay ‘The Cure for Psychoanalysis’ and points out that Milner was amongst those, together with Bion, ‘who would claim that too certain a destination as itself a saboteur of psychoanalytic treatment.’ (Phillips, 2021, p.150-151) I would like to see something of this negotiation with the word.

PATIENT PERSPECTIVES, SOCIAL IDENTITY, PSYCHOTHERAPY, QUALITATIVE PSYCHOANALYTIC METHOD

The process of psychotherapy invites the patient to explore their mind and the mind of the other but does so in the context of a therapeutic relationship in which the therapist is at least partly unknown. This article explores how patients, unbeknown to their therapist, explore clues that may disclose some knowledge about their therapists. One route towards exploring the unknown is through the therapist's social identities. The article presents an analysis of interviews conducted with 11 patients attending a free clinic in Johannesburg, South Africa. Their process of exploring the therapist and encountering the unknown, and wondering about whether their therapist can know them, is presented. The therapist's social identities offer a ‘glimpse’ into the therapist's mind. The article offers an alternative way of approaching inadvertent self-disclosure and invites therapists to be aware of their patients’ explorations of them that may remain unknown to therapists. Social identity offers a potential vehicle for alienation but also for connection.

Philip Hewitt  

In this timely book, that is warmly welcomed by distinguished scholars on its sleeve, Dr Carla Penna describes the development of theories of group psychologies over the last century, during which there have been many social upheavals and distinct changes to theory, all of which were influential to the field.

However, before getting to the more contemporary material, Penna first describes the beginning of social experience in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Century plagues, showing how in their own way they sowed the seeds of modern theoretical formulations of social processes. She also shows how these perspectives developed in the Eighteenth Century, familiarly known as ‘The Age of Enlightenment’, with an increasing recognition of the human capacity for sensing individuality, identity and, ultimately, social phenomena on a larger scale. This sets the scene for an unfolding understanding of the developing complexity of crowd, large group, herd and popular social movement to the present time. From here, any reader will consider the present Covid 19 pandemic, international conflicts and the dramatic changes occurring with increasing use of ‘factualising’ trans-global digital communications.

Following this account of early social theory, the development of crowd psychology and dynamics of the large group within the nineteenth century then begins to give shape to our current understanding. This account is picked up carefully through reference to principal theorists and the dramatic times through which they lived. This succinctly illustrates how a growing idea of ‘the individual’, both in terms of expectations and recognition, was central to theoretical developments. One of the most striking features of this account is the impact of industrialisation in the nineteenth century leading up to the First World War and after. As is well referenced in the book, these times had the most profound effects on society. They were crucial in the search for the sorts of existential meanings that are so central to understandings emerging in the later part of the twentieth century.

Barry Richards

Poole, UK
brichards@bournemouth.ac.uk

Barry Richards  

What connections might there be between the lives of a mixed-race seamstress/governess in mid-19th century Kingston, Jamaica, and a white domestic servant in early 20th-century London? Henrietta Dawson and Alice Triggs are two of the case studies in this new book by Peter Barham, across nearly all of whom there was a deep connection: subjection to the abusive psychiatric regimes of their times. Their experiences were of course different. Dawson was taken to the Kingston Lunatic Asylum during an acute depressive episode in 1858. She recovered, and wrote about the ordeals which she had suffered and seen others undergo in the brutal asylum. Triggs was beset by depression and anxiety throughout her life, and from 1915 was a ‘revolving door’ patient in Colney Hatch and Napsbury Lunatic Asylums, receiving no real care or attention, before spending over 40 years at Napsbury until her death there in 1962. Both were from modest backgrounds, though not destitute. Dawson was the daughter of a lawyer, one of the colonial white men who gave ongoing financial support to the offspring of their liaisons with black women. Triggs’ working-class parents died while she was in her teens, but her siblings appear to have been upwardly mobile, in contrast to her own fate.

These and other richly detailed case studies are at the core of Barham's book, much of which builds on his previous work about connecting with and respecting the life-worlds of those now called ‘service users’, especially those labouring under diagnoses of psychosis. In this latest study, the author's interdisciplinary skill in weaving together psychology, history and sociology are deployed in his case analyses. But while focussed empirically on individual examples, he aims to show how within Britain and its empire a particular set of values has been at the centre both of the state's management of psychological distress and of the white racism characteristic of the imperial period. The clue to the content of these values is in the book's title. Barham does not explicitly unpack the phrase ‘outrageous reason’, but he does not need to. The message he draws from his case studies and develops into an overall narrative is that a moralistic model of rationality underpinned both racism and, as it emerged in the 19th century to shape the state's response to a range of problems, psychiatry. At the centre of this model was an image of ‘reason’, reflecting the outlook, behaviours and values of the dominant classes within Britain of the high imperial era.

Konstantin Nemirovskiy  

Introduction

The Clinical Commentaries have been part of the British Journal of Psychotherapy from the beginning. They featured as a section in the first issue in 1984 and went through to 2007. After a gap of 9 years, their presence was renewed by Ann Horne and Mark Budden when the new series of Commentaries appeared, which now provides readers with an opportunity to engage (or ‘play’) via a detailed examination of a piece of clinical work and thereby articulate their own perspectives in relation to those of the commentators.

The clinical material and its discussion implies two types of freedom—for the clinician, who does so anonymously and with respect for patient confidentiality, and for the commentators, who discuss it independently of each other and in a format of free association rather than supervision. This enables the recreation in part of the process unfolding within the real session and in the clinician's mind.

Given the lack of inter-school comparisons in psychoanalysis and psychotherapy, it was innovative at the time of the Journal's inception and continues to be so to this day. There were two reasons for this. After the UK psychotherapy split in the 1970s into an increasing number of separate organisations which often did not talk to each other, it was important to find a platform to bring these diverse opinions back into communication and offer some sort of comparison. Another aim was to help psychotherapists express their opinion, which was not easy at a time when most of the papers were published by psychoanalysts. However, regardless of qualifications, we all work with the clinical material and the Journal could become an important place to start and wade into theoretical discussion (Robert Hinshelwood, 2024, personal communication).

The commentators who have generously been part of over 30-plus years have included not only representatives of more than just three British schools (Freudian, Kleinian or Independent) but also Lacanians, group-analysts, interpersonalists and Jungians. In addition, specialists from other approaches such as gestalt, humanistic, integrative, family and organisational counsellors have voiced their opinions in the pages of the Journal.

Alan Baban MBBS MA MRCPsych , Thomas Hillen MD MA phil MPH MRCPsych , Giles Story MA MB BChir PHD MRCPsych , Wendy Burn BM MMedSc FRCPsych and Vivienne Curtis MBBS frcpsych FAoME

Vivienne Curtis

alanbaban@nhs.net

Vivienne Curtis   Consultant Psychiatrist at South London and Maudsley NHS Trust, Head of the London School of Psychiatry, Associate Dean for Academic Psychiatry at RCPsych, Visiting Senior Lecturer at King's College London, and a Visiting Professor at University of Bolton, UK
COVID-19, PSYCHOTHERAPY, PSYCHIATRY, REMOTE WORK, TRAINING

Acquiring competence in psychotherapy is a mandatory part of psychiatric training in the UK. Within their first 3 years of ‘Core Psychiatry’ training, doctors are expected to deliver both short-term and long-term psychotherapy treatments, supervised by the local Medical Psychotherapy tutor. During the Covid-19 pandemic, these treatments and their supervisions were carried out remotely. This pan-London qualitative research study, commissioned by the Health Education England London School of Psychiatry, aimed to explore trainees’ and trainers’ experiences of the psychotherapy curriculum within Core Psychiatric training, as well as their experiences of remote work during the pandemic. Seventeen participants were interviewed (out of 19 who came forward), including both trainees and trainers working within the London region. Thematic analysis of the transcripts of the semi-structured interviews identified five main themes with associated sub-themes. The results suggest that trainees found their psychotherapy experience to be enriching. However, there is work to be done around barriers and anxieties faced by trainees, for instance concerning the impact of patient drop out on training progression. Remote work posed additional issues for trainers and trainees in addressing psychotherapy competencies, with feelings of disconnection and loss being prominent.

Editorial November 2024

Gary Winship

Gary Winship

Nottingham, UK
gary.winship@nottingham.ac.uk

Gary Winship  

Announcements

As well as reporting on the British Journal of Psychotherapy's 40th Birthday conference and notice about the editorial board, this editorial also carries two obituaries by Brett Kahr for our colleagues Camila Batmanghelidjh and Derek Draper, both of whom passed away earlier this year, and both were psychotherapists who were well-known in the public sphere.

The 40th birthday celebration conference of the British Journal of Psychotherapy (BJP) over the summer was a great opportunity to consider the role of a psychotherapy journal in supporting the continuity of knowledge exchange in the field of psychotherapy and also its role as space for debate with all of the disruption that might come in tow. In her keynote address in the morning of the conference, Helen Morgan spoke about the perils of the way in which some people ‘avoided potentially disruptive thought’. Helen argued that psychoanalysis has much to offer when it comes to understanding the deep troubles of our times; however, she argued that the revolutionary concepts of psychoanalysis, as well as its conformist inclinations, make psychoanalysis vulnerable to destructive forces, not only from without but also from within. She advocated for a critical approach, and while accepting the formidable intelligence and legacy of our psychoanalytic predecessors, she pointed to the necessity of ‘humility and holding our truths lightly’. This, Helen said, entails saving the world ‘one patient at a time’.

David Black's keynote set out a persuasive case for foregrounding ethics in all of our work, pointing to work of the French philosopher Emmanuel Levinas. Levinas's concept of the ‘face of the other’, David argued, offered a selfless proposition that moved ethics beyond a self-centred set of rules or procedures to be followed. Instead, the ‘face of the other’ creates a matricial space (Chetrit-Vatine, 2004) that is the primary source of an imbued ethical fabric in infant and child development through non-oppressive parenting that facilitates the development for respect, duty, justice, courage, friendship and a capacity to receive love and respond to others.

Rose Baring  

Andrew Feldmár, a Hungarian-Canadian psychotherapist now in his 80s, is widely published in Hungary. This translation of his open-hearted autobiography and account of the beliefs which have influenced the way he has lived his life and practiced his profession is his first book in English. It is a wide-ranging exploration of the people and texts—philosophical, anthropological and psychological—that have been most influential in his life.

628

As the title suggests, his ideas were profoundly affected by the Scottish psychiatrist and controversialist psychotherapist R. D. Laing, with whom he spent a heady year in 1974-1975 and whose role in questioning the psychiatric orthodoxies of the mid-20th century made him a leading figure in the counterculture of that time. Feldmár's Journal Entries from that period are the most fascinating part of the book, a form of time travel which throws us headfirst with him into the life of the shelters set up by Laing and his colleagues in the Philadelphia Association (PA), to house psychiatric patients in an environment which challenged the prevailing repressive ideas about mental health and illness. Feldmár has practiced a radical psychotherapy based on a Laingian anti-authoritarian ethos ever since—listening closely to the patient to help them discover how it is that they want to lead their life. Reading this text now allows us to experience something of how he got there.

It is not always a straight-forward read; however, taking my queue from Feldmár himself when he described his approach to some of the theoretical writing recommended by colleagues in London, I found the best way to read Credo was as if ‘I were swimming in it. If I don't agree with something or I don't understand something, I just swim through it and concern myself with the things I find interesting’. (142 p.) After all, the book is such a clarion call to individual freedom, to therapy as ‘a process by which patients find their own path’, (286 p.) that this feels in keeping with its spirit.

Neil Morgan

London, UK

Neil Morgan  

David Shaddock, a published poet and inter-subjectivist psychotherapist, has written a book with an intriguing title. Aiming in a general way at inspiring clinical work, he wants to open an imaginative space between the patient and analyst on one side and the poet and reader on the other.

636

Poetry has not always had a good press in terms of creativity. Plato, for example, argued strongly that art and poetry are extremely bad for us. He gives this view a trial run in Ion, which is an argument with a rhapsode (that is a poetry reciter), of that name (Plato (Saunders ed.), 1987). A fuller account of his disagreement with them is given in Books III and X of The Republic (Cornford, 1941, see also Murdoch, 1977). He argues that Art is always bad for us because it is only imitation and copying. Poets who recite emotions in a similar way are detrimental to the psyche, for how could a thing without a rational account ever lead to knowledge?

However, the good news for the reputation of poets is that, particularly from the nineteenth century onwards, things have moved full circle. The pivotal turning point was probably Coleridge's doctrine of the Imagination, which made feeling the key to interpreting life (Coleridge, 1985; Holmes, 1982).

To skip ahead from poetry to psychoanalysis, one can link the process of Coleridge's Imagination with Wilfred Bion's key idea of alpha function. Both concepts can transform our experience and help us develop. Both are a sort of combination of a Noah's Ark for feeling and a rocket launch pad for mental growth. Contrast with Coleridge's Imagination, a poor cousin he called fancy—a depressingly less symbolic, less alive, activity that simply rearranged things in the mind as counters (as in a game of draughts) but which can pass itself off as Imagination at first glance. This is the difference between what M. H. Abrams famously called The Mirror and the Lamp—imitation versus the internal illumination of emotional inspiration (Abrams, 1953).

Of course, what is really at stake here is meaning itself (and the meaning of meaning) and the role of feeling in generating it. In the last 50 years, psychoanalysts have much expanded our knowledge in this area, most centrally through their work on symbolization.

MRS KLEIN: Tears, you know, are very much equated with excreta in the unconscious mind. Through tears the mourner casts bad objects into the outside world.

From Mrs Klein, a play written by Nicholas Wright, 1988.

639

What happens to the struggling psyche when tears are not available? Raffaella Hilty has previously explored an interest in bodily communications in an article originally published in the British Journal of Psychotherapy in 2020 and included here in a slightly extended form (Hilty, 2020). Within this, she describes work with a patient, ‘Mark’, who communicates his unloved state in the form of an almost unbearable stench. She comes to understand the smell as ‘an expression of embodied memories communicating traumatic experiences of early physical and emotional neglect, as well as evacuating the toxicity of these experiences’ (p. 99). I was struck by her ability to meld traditional psychoanalytic concepts with this area—human body odour—that might be overlooked or too embarrassing to stay with.

The current volume takes that interest further, gathering a collection of papers that explore the ways that the body becomes the mode of communication, whether through smell, physical actions such as spitting, excreting, masturbation or via eating disorders, which are included as ‘an expression of the use of the body to communicate unbearable psychic distress’ (p. xxviii).

Hilty addresses the problematic aspects of the term ‘primitive’ with its connotations of inferiority, and of colonial racism, explaining that ‘this book does not refer to bodily communications as primitive because we see them as inferior to verbal language, but simply because they point to the beginnings of psychological development’ (p. xxvi). Some of the clinical material describes people who are institutionalised, and marginalised, in society, and is therefore different in character to work where, in one case, the therapist collaborates with the patient to think together about their long-term therapeutic relationship (William F. Cornell, pp. 157-180). For me, the most moving papers were about patients with little or no effective voice.

María Eugenia Rodríguez

María Eugenia Rodríguez

meucidro.efpp@gmail.com

María Eugenia Rodríguez  

First of all, I would like to thank our colleague for the generosity of sharing a clinical experience and providing me the opportunity to think about it.

The therapist introduces us to S., a middle-aged man who comes for consultation because he doesn't understand his feelings towards others, always highlighting 276 isolation and lack of contact. In his internal world's description, a ‘normal’ relationship with his mother appears to be one ‘in which there was no intimacy of any kind’. So far, the patient tells us about a failure of early emotional and intimate relationships, a process which would have been essential for his constitution and growth as a subject.

He lacks in his early experiences what Klein called ‘unconscious oneness’: ‘based on the unconscious of the mother and of the child being in close relation to each other. The infant's resultant feeling of being understood underlies the first and fundamental relation in his life—the relation to the mother’ (Klein, 1959, p. 248). Bion will add the containment experience and the container-contained relationship.

As we get to know the patient, a first clinical reflection is that this lack of intimacy prevents him from being nourished from emotional experiences and in turn feeding those experiences. On the contrary, he cannot reach, feel or understand emotions. He does not feel loved, understood, or contained by anyone and he cannot do it with others either. He thus lives an ‘extremely poorly’ existence, continually concerned with himself, concerned with the survival of his self, remaining distant and inaccessible, as stated by a pathological identification with the maternal object and the relationship with it. This internal impoverishment, with little symbolic function, also prevents him from developing a true dialogue with its internal and external objects; it prevents him from containing conflicts with objects and tolerating loneliness.

On the other hand, the patient tells us that the paternal relationship was dominated by hatred and destructiveness. S. interprets the suicide of his alcoholic father, who fell from the balcony being drunk, as the father ‘mistook the door for a window and hung for some time clinging to the edge of the balcony, but no one came to help’.

Laurence Spurling , Jan Hepburn and Ronald Doctor

Ronald Doctor

janhep@gmail.com

Ronald Doctor   Consultant psychiatrist in medical psychotherapy, West London Mental Health NHS Trust, and has a Private Psychoanalytical Practice. He is a Fellow of the British Psychoanalytical Society, Senior Member of the British Psychotherapy Foundation, Chair of the IPA Committee of Psychoanalysis and Law, Board Member of the International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy and Fellow of the Royal College of Psychiatrists. He has edited two books: Dangerous Patients: A Psychodynamic Approach to Risk Assessmentand Management (London: Routledge, 2003) and Murder: A Psychotherapeutic Investigation (London: Routledge, 2008), contributed chapters to numerous books, including Psychoanalysis, Law and Society and published articles including, History, murder and the fear of death, International Journal of Applied Psychoanalytical Studies (Wiley, 2015)
SESSION FREQUENCY, COMPARATIVE, METHOD, TECHNIQUE, WORKING MODEL

This is an exploratory account of an applied clinical method, the Comparative Clinical Method, used to address a specific question: how can we best think of the difference between intensive and non-intensive analytic work? Normally, it is session frequency that is taken as a determining difference, as a marker of a different approach or method being employed. In our investigation, which consisted of the three authors presenting examples of their clinical work to each other, we did not find the intensive and non-intensive work of each author to demonstrate clear and easily defined differences in method or technique. Instead, we found more evidence of each author adopting a coherent and consistent approach, based on an underlying and implicit working model, across their intensive and non-intensive work. We conclude from this that the differences between intensive and non-intensive work are best explored by encouraging more conceptually rigorous and clinically specific descriptions of the different kinds of analytic assumptions and methods employed in ordinary analytic clinical work.
